dct_description_sm: Modifications in vegetation structure in Northern ecosystems due to climate change may result in feedback to warming by various processes including: alteration of the surface energy balance, modification of precipitation regimes, permafrost degradation and increased nutrient availability. Soil nutrients are expected to become more available to plants under warmer climatic conditions. How Arctic plants are going to respond to higher nutrient availability remains a central question only partially answered to date. Shrub cover increase has been reported from sub-Arctic areas underlain by discontinuous permafrost in Nunavik, as well as across much of the Low Arctic. However the response is very heterogeneous at the landscape scale, with some areas showing a great increase while others have hardly changed. Nutrient availability is mainly controlled by micro-environmental conditions (e.g. soil temperature, litter quality, soil moisture) which influence the activity of soil microorganisms. It is important to understand that these conditions may differ locally in any given area. Our main objective is to evaluate the growth of Betula glandulosa Michx in relation to the nutrient availability in sites near Umiujaq (Nunavik), where shrub cover has greatly increased versus other sites that have only slightly changed in the last 20 years.
dct_title_s: Response to Climate Change: Shrub growth, soil nutrients and microclimate data at Umiujaq, Nunavik
